Summary: Rust 1.0 was released on May 15, 2015. The release marked a significant milestone for the language, with the vast majority of the standard library now stable, and many popular crates on crates.io working on the stable release channel. The release also included changes such as arithmetic on basic integer types checking for overflow in debug builds, the removal of generic numeric traits, and the stabilization of many APIs in `std`. The focus of Rust 2015, the default edition, was on stability, ensuring a solid foundation for building large software projects.

    ### 1.0.0

# 1.0.0 #

>  Released on: 15 May, 2015
>  Branched from master on: 4 December, 2015

 ~1500 changes, numerous bugfixes

## Highlights #

 The vast majority of the standard library is now `#[stable]`. It is no longer possible to use unstable features with a stable build of the compiler.
 Many popular crates on crates.io now work on the stable release channel.
 Arithmetic on basic integer types now checks for overflow in debug builds.

## Language # [...] Generic numeric traits were completely removed. This was made possible thanks to inherent methods for primitive types, and the removal gives maximal flexibility for designing a numeric hierarchy in the future.
 The `Fn` traits are now related via inheritance and provide ergonomic blanket implementations.
 The `Index` and `IndexMut` traits were changed to take the index by value, enabling code like `hash_map["string"]` to work. [...] The path API was revised to normalize `.`, adjusting the tradeoffs in favor of the most common usage.
 A large number of remaining APIs in `std` were also stabilized during this cycle; about 75% of the non-deprecated API surface is now stable.
 The new string pattern API landed, which makes the string slice API much more internally consistent and flexible.
 A new set of generic conversion traits replaced many existing ad hoc traits.
